messages.author: e74863d19d180366
messages.subject: setting three constraints to a parameter vector
parts:
Hello everyone, 

I am dealing with a stochastic mortality model, I have four vectors of parameters, K1, K2,K3,G4, where Ks are of length m and G4=(g_1,...,g_n) of length n.
I am setting three constraints to G4, such that for c=1,...,n,  sum_{c=1}^{n} (g_c)=0, sum_{c=1}^{n} (c*g_c)=0, sum_{c=1}^{n} (square(c)*g_c)=0 and not sure how to deal with the last two constraints. 
Can I adjust the updated samples for G4 after each iteration to make sure the constrains are satisfied and make corresponding adjustment to the Ks. Then the adjusted samples are used for next iteration.
 Does stan allow to do so and where can I put the code for that?

Thanks a million 

Liang

Hi Daniel

for(i in 1:m)
for(j in 1:n)
mhat[i,j] <- log(1+exp(kappa_1[i]+kappa_2[i]*beta2v[j]+kappa_3[i]*beta3v[j]+gamma_par[n+i-j]));

for(i in 1:m)
for(j in 1:n)
dtx[i,j] ~ poisson(etx[i,j]*mhat[i,j]);

the kappa_1,2,3 are parameter vectors. The gamma_par is the parameter vector that makes trouble.

sum g_c=0; sum c*g_c=0; sum c^2*g_c=0
I am giving non-informative prior for all the parameter vectors as long as they satisfy the above constraints.
I am not sure how to do it

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] setting three constraints to a parameter vector
parts:
The problem is how to define such a program!
What we want is a parameter or transformed parameter

vector[N] theta;

satisfying the following three constraints:

1. SUM_{n in 1:N} theta[n] == 0

2. SUM_{n in 1:N} n * theta[n] == 0

3. SUM_{n in 1:N} n^2 * theta[n] == 0

I don't know how to do that or even if it's possible. For
any one of the constraints, you let theta[1:(N-1)] be
free and set theta[N] accordingly. I don't know how to
satisfy all three simultaneously or how you'd do the
Jacobian.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] setting three constraints to a parameter vector
parts:
You can’t do a Jacobian because the transformation
isn’t an isomorphism (you’re trying to map the plane
into a sphere, which always leaves some points
messed up). Alternatively, if you try to calculate a
Jacobian you’ll see that you end up with an infinite
number of terms that contribute.

Geometrically, this is trying to find the intersections
of multiple spheres with varying radii along the
principle directions. As Bob notes, this might not
even be possible (but maybe at theta[1] = 1,
theta[\1] = 0?), and even if it were you’d end up
with a disjoint space.

But this also smells of a bad, non-generative model
that we probably don’t want to be messing with
anyways. Like some optimization problem that’s
trying to be forced into an ill-posed probabilistic
problem, or some “measurements” that are assumed
to be infinitely informative.

Thanks everyone for the detailed answers. I considered fixing the starting value before but the intuitive meaning of doing this is hard to explain to the industry. In practice I replaced these constraints with something else as I also found it was not possible to directly apply them.

Thanks a million
On 11 Nov 2016, 20:02 +0000, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu>, wrote:

Thanks. That's what I was afraid of. I hadn't looked at these constrained problems in a while.

Liang, if you can write out the constraint for a1, then a2 as a function of a1, etc. then it's straightforward.

On Nov 11, 2016, at 2:42 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

You can’t do a Jacobian because the transformation
isn’t an isomorphism (you’re trying to map the plane
into a sphere, which always leaves some points
messed up). Alternatively, if you try to calculate a
Jacobian you’ll see that you end up with an infinite
number of terms that contribute.

Geometrically, this is trying to find the intersections
of multiple spheres with varying radii along the
principle directions. As Bob notes, this might not
even be possible (but maybe at theta[1] = 1,
theta[\1] = 0?), and even if it were you’d end up
with a disjoint space.

But this also smells of a bad, non-generative model
that we probably don’t want to be messing with
anyways. Like some optimization problem that’s
trying to be forced into an ill-posed probabilistic
problem, or some “measurements” that are assumed
to be infinitely informative.

On Nov 11, 2016, at 11:33 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

The problem is how to define such a program!
What we want is a parameter or transformed parameter

vector[N] theta;

satisfying the following three constraints:

1. SUM_{n in 1:N} theta[n] == 0

2. SUM_{n in 1:N} n * theta[n] == 0

3. SUM_{n in 1:N} n^2 * theta[n] == 0

I don't know how to do that or even if it's possible. For
any one of the constraints, you let theta[1:(N-1)] be
free and set theta[N] accordingly. I don't know how to
satisfy all three simultaneously or how you'd do the
Jacobian.

- Bob

On Nov 11, 2016, at 1:17 PM, Liang Chen <liang....@gmail.com> wrote:


Hello everyone,

I am dealing with a stochastic mortality model, I have four vectors of parameters, K1, K2,K3,G4, where Ks are of length m and G4=(g_1,...,g_n) of length n.
I am setting three constraints to G4, such that for c=1,...,n, sum_{c=1}^{n} (g_c)=0, sum_{c=1}^{n} (c*g_c)=0, sum_{c=1}^{n} (square(c)*g_c)=0 and not sure how to deal with the last two constraints.
Can I adjust the updated samples for G4 after each iteration to make sure the constrains are satisfied and make corresponding adjustment to the Ks. Then the adjusted samples are used for next iteration.
Does stan allow to do so and where can I put the code for that?

Thanks a million

Liang

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] setting three constraints to a parameter vector
parts:
On Friday, November 11, 2016 at 2:33:40 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
The problem is how to define such a program!
What we want is a parameter or transformed parameter

  vector[N] theta;

satisfying the following three constraints:

1.  SUM_{n in 1:N} theta[n] == 0

2.  SUM_{n in 1:N} n * theta[n] == 0

3.  SUM_{n in 1:N} n^2 * theta[n] == 0

I don't know how to do that or even if it's possible.  For
any one of the constraints, you let theta[1:(N-1)] be
free and set theta[N] accordingly.  I don't know how to
satisfy all three simultaneously or how you'd do the
Jacobian.

If you declare in parameters

vector[N - 3] theta_free;

and then in in transformed parameters you start with

vector[N] theta;
theta[1:(N - 3)] = theta_free;

and then you have three equations that along with theta_free pin down the three remaining elements of theta.

Ben
